a: Satan
t: Satan, an adversary, or the LORD?
p: 2 Samuel 24:1 says the LORD stirred David up. Chronicles says Satan did. Readers explain the change in four main ways.
b: Samuel opens the story, "The LORD's anger burned against Israel once more. He stirred David up against them" (2 Samuel 24:1). Chronicles puts satan in God's place. (1) A personal adversary. Most Jewish and Christian readers take this as the heavenly Satan, acting only with God's leave, as in Job 1–2 and 1 Kings 22:19–23; both books are then true at once. (2) A human adversary. The word has no article, so it may mean "an adversary" of any kind. Sara Japhet leaves it open; John Sailhamer argued for an enemy army whose threat moved David to count his troops. (3) A heavenly attacker, not yet the devil. Peggy Day and Ryan Stokes read a member of God's court sent to harm, like the angel who stood in Balaam's road "as an adversary" (Numbers 22:22). (4) A later theology. Many critical scholars think the Chronicler, writing after the exile, would not say that God moved a king to sin, and so named another agent. See the chapter page and the topic on Satan.
r: 2 Samuel 24:1; Job 1:6–12; Job 2:1–7; Zechariah 3:1–2; Numbers 22:22; 1 Kings 22:19–23; James 1:13

a: stirred David up
t: The same verb as in Job
p: The verb sut, 'incite', is the one the satan's work is described with in Job 2:3.
b: Chronicles keeps Samuel's verb, vayyaset, "and he incited." It is a word for pushing someone into a course they would not have taken: Jezebel "incited" Ahab (1 Kings 21:25), and in Job God tells the satan, "you lured me against him" (Job 2:3). That link may be why the Chronicler found Satan a natural subject for the verb. The phrase "stood up against" is used of an enemy rising to attack (compare Daniel 8:25; 11:14).

a: from Beersheba as far as Dan
p: Samuel says 'from Dan to Beersheba'. Chronicles turns the phrase around and starts with Judah's south.
b: The usual formula for the whole land runs north to south, "from Dan to Beersheba" (Judges 20:1; 2 Samuel 24:2). Chronicles writes "from Beersheba to Dan" here and in 2 Chronicles 30:5. Many commentators see the writer's point of view: he lived in Judah, and the land is seen from Jerusalem outward. Chronicles also drops the long route of the counters given in 2 Samuel 24:5–8 and the nine months and twenty days.

a: Why should it become guilt for Israel?
p: Joab's last question is Chronicles' own. Its word for guilt, ashmah, is a favorite of writers after the exile.
b: In Samuel, Joab asks only why the king wants this (2 Samuel 24:3). Chronicles adds that the count will bring ashmah, "guilt," on all Israel. The word is rare before the exile and common in Chronicles and Ezra (Ezra 9:6–7, 9:13, 9:15; Ezra 10:10; 2 Chronicles 24:18; 2 Chronicles 28:13; 2 Chronicles 33:23). It turns a royal mistake into something that endangers the community, which is exactly what happens in 21:14. Joab, the hard soldier of Samuel, here speaks as the people's conscience.
r: 2 Samuel 24:3; Ezra 9:6; Ezra 10:10; 2 Chronicles 24:18; 2 Chronicles 28:13; 2 Chronicles 33:23

a: a million and a hundred thousand
p: Samuel counts 800,000 and 500,000. Chronicles counts 1,100,000 and 470,000. Neither fits the land in David's day easily.
b: The note on 2 Samuel 24:9 sets out the usual explanations: different groups counted, copying errors, 'elef meaning a unit rather than a thousand, or numbers that were never meant as head counts. One old harmony adds the standing army of 27:1–15 (twelve divisions of 24,000, or 288,000) to Samuel's 800,000, which gives about 1,100,000. Chronicles' lower figure for Judah could reflect its remark that Benjamin was not counted (21:6). Archaeological surveys suggest a population for the whole region in the 900s BC well under a million.

a: Levi and Benjamin he did not enroll with the rest
t: Why Levi and Benjamin were left out
p: Only Chronicles says the count skipped two tribes. Levi was never counted for war. Benjamin is harder to explain.
b: The Law kept Levi out of the military count (Numbers 1:47–49), so Joab was keeping a rule. Benjamin may have been skipped because Jerusalem and Gibeon, where the tabernacle stood (21:29), were in or near its territory, or because the count was cut short (27:24 says Joab never finished). Chronicles gives Joab's own reason: he found the order abhorrent. The verb ta'av is the root of to'evah, the word the Law uses for what God finds abhorrent (Deuteronomy 7:25–26).

a: and he struck Israel
p: The verse sums up the outcome in advance. Some readers take it as a first, separate blow.
b: Hebrew stories often state the result first and then tell how it came about. On that reading "he struck Israel" points ahead to the plague of 21:14. Others, following some Jewish commentators, see a first warning blow that brings David to confess in 21:8. In Samuel, David's own conscience strikes him (2 Samuel 24:10). Chronicles moves the initiative to God, who judges the deed as wrong before David admits it.

a: Gad, David's visionary
p: Chronicles calls Gad simply 'David's visionary' (chozeh).
b: Samuel calls Gad both "the prophet" and "David's visionary" (2 Samuel 24:11). Chronicles keeps only chozeh, "visionary," the title it gives Gad again in 29:29, where he stands beside "Samuel the seer" and "Nathan the prophet." Gad first appears with David during his flight from Saul (1 Samuel 22:5). Chronicles says he helped set up the temple music (2 Chronicles 29:25).

a: I am holding out three things to you
p: Samuel has notel, 'lay on'; Chronicles has noteh, 'hold out, offer'. The words differ by one letter.
b: In 2 Samuel 24:12 God says notel, "I am laying (three things) on you." Chronicles reads noteh, "I am stretching out, offering." The Hebrew letters lamed and he are not easily confused, so one writer may have chosen the other word on purpose, but no one can be sure which came first. The sense is close either way: David is given a choice of punishments.

a: three years of hunger
p: Samuel's Hebrew says seven years of famine. Chronicles, like the Greek of Samuel, says three.
b: The Masoretic Text of 2 Samuel 24:13 offers "seven years" of famine. The Greek of Samuel and Chronicles both read "three years," which makes a neat set: three years, three months, three days. This is one of many places where Chronicles agrees with a Samuel text other than the one in our printed Hebrew Bibles. The Plain English of Samuel keeps its own Hebrew, and this verse keeps Chronicles' Hebrew. See the variant on 2 Samuel 24:13.

a: three days of the LORD's sword, pestilence in the land, with the LORD's angel bringing ruin
p: Chronicles adds the sword and the angel to the third choice. Both return later in the story.
b: Samuel offers "three days of pestilence" (2 Samuel 24:13). Chronicles calls the plague "the LORD's sword" and names the destroying angel in advance. The sword appears in the angel's hand in 21:16, goes back in its sheath in 21:27, and still frightens David in 21:30, so the addition ties the chapter together. The "destroyer" of the Passover night is in the background (Exodus 12:23), as is the angel who struck Assyria's army (2 Kings 19:35).

a: let me fall into the LORD's hand
t: Into the hands of the Lord
p: Ben Sira repeats David's words around 180 BC as advice for every believer.
b: David's choice became a proverb. Ben Sira, a Jerusalem teacher writing in Hebrew about 180 BC, says, "Let us fall into the hands of the Lord and not into human hands, for as his greatness is, so is his mercy" (Sirach 2:18). Chronicles adds "very" to God's compassion. The note on 2 Samuel 24:14 explains why David preferred a plague: it came straight from God.

a: the LORD saw
p: The text does not say. The Talmud answers: he saw the ashes of Isaac on this very mountain.
b: Chronicles adds the words "the LORD saw" before he relents. The rabbis asked what he saw. In Bavli Berakhot 62b, Rav says he saw Jacob (Genesis 32:2); Shmuel says he saw "the ashes of Isaac," reading this hill as Moriah, where Abraham said, "God will see" (Genesis 22:8, 22:14); others say he saw the half-shekel ransom, or the future temple. Christian and modern readers usually take it simply: God saw the suffering and took pity. Either way the story connects God's "seeing" with this place, which 2 Chronicles 3:1 calls Mount Moriah.

a: he regretted the harm
p: The verb nicham is the same as in Samuel. Here God relents while the angel is still at work.
b: God's "regret" or "change of mind" (nicham) is discussed in the note on 2 Samuel 24:16 and on the topic page on God's regret. Chronicles sharpens the timing: "as he was ruining it," the LORD saw and relented. Mercy breaks in during the judgment, before David has prayed (21:17).

a: Ornan the Jebusite
p: Chronicles always spells the name Ornan. Samuel spells it several ways, most often Araunah.
b: The landowner's name is spelled four or more ways in the Hebrew of Samuel and in the Dead Sea scroll 4QSam-a (see the note on 2 Samuel 24:16). Chronicles regularly has Ornan, and the Greek of Chronicles has Orna. Many scholars think the name is a Hurrian title meaning "lord." The Jebusites held Jerusalem before David took it (11:4–6), so the temple's site was bought from one of the city's old inhabitants.

a: standing between earth and sky
t: A scene the Dead Sea scroll shares
p: The angel with the drawn sword is missing in the Masoretic Samuel but seems to have stood in the Qumran Samuel scroll.
b: For a long time scholars thought the Chronicler invented this vivid scene. Then fragments of 4QSam-a, a copy of Samuel from about 50–25 BC, were found to contain words matching this verse, including the elders "covered in sackcloth." How much of it the scroll really preserves is debated (see the variant on 2 Samuel 24:16), but many now think the Chronicler copied it from the Samuel text he had. If so, this is not a change made by Chronicles but a passage lost from the Masoretic Samuel, perhaps when a scribe's eye skipped. The first sentence of the Plain English here is word for word the reading shown in the 2 Samuel variant. The second sentence differs from that variant on purpose: the scroll, as reconstructed, is reported to name only the elders, not David, and to order the words differently, so the English differs too.

a: his sword drawn in his hand
t: The angel with a drawn sword
p: The same picture meets Balaam and Joshua. In Balaam's story the angel is called 'an adversary', satan.
b: Balaam's donkey "saw the angel of the LORD standing in the road with his sword drawn in his hand" (Numbers 22:23), and that angel "stood in the road as an adversary against him" (Numbers 22:22). Joshua met "a man holding a drawn sword" (Joshua 5:13). Ryan Stokes argues that the Chronicler knew Balaam's story and that the "satan" of 21:1 and the sword-bearing angel are best read as the same kind of being: a heavenly attacker sent by God. Most readers keep the two distinct.

a: covered in sackcloth
p: Rough goat-hair cloth was worn in mourning and in prayer for mercy.
b: Sackcloth was coarse, dark cloth, usually of goat hair, worn next to the skin by mourners and by people pleading with God (Genesis 37:34; 1 Kings 21:27; Jonah 3:5–8; Joel 1:13). The elders join David in repentance for the whole city. In Chronicles' own day, Ezra and Nehemiah's assemblies did the same (Nehemiah 9:1).

a: It is I who sinned and did great evil
p: The Hebrew may hide the word 'shepherd': 'I the shepherd did evil'. See the variant.
b: In 2 Samuel 24:17 the Greek and, it seems, 4QSam-a read "I the shepherd did wrong," which fits "these sheep" in the next breath. Chronicles' Hebrew, vehara' hare'oti, "and I have surely done evil," uses nearly the same letters as haro'eh hare'oti, "I the shepherd did evil." Many scholars think the shepherd stood in the Chronicler's text too. David, the shepherd boy made king (17:7), asks to bear the blow for his flock.

a: please turn your hand against me and against my father's family
p: Like Moses after the golden calf, David asks to be struck in his people's place.
b: If God would not forgive the people, Moses prayed, "wipe me out, please, from your book that you have written" (Exodus 32:32). David asks that the punishment fall on him and his own family, "not against your people." Chronicles adds the last words, which make the plea sharper. Christian readers have heard in it the good shepherd who gives his life for the sheep (John 10:11).

a: the LORD's angel told Gad
t: An angel speaks to a prophet
p: In Chronicles the angel, not Gad, gives the command. Angels pass on God's word to prophets in Zechariah too.
b: Samuel says only that Gad came to David (2 Samuel 24:18). Chronicles has the angel give Gad the order. Angels that speak to prophets are a feature of books written after the exile, above all Zechariah 1–6, where "the angel who was talking with me" explains each vision. Chronicles here reflects the same world.

a: Ornan had been threshing wheat
t: Threshing wheat when the angel comes
p: Gideon too was beating out wheat when the angel of the LORD appeared. 4QSam-a is reported to have this detail.
b: "His son Gideon was beating out wheat in the winepress" when the angel of the LORD came to him (Judges 6:11), and in Gideon's story too fire from the rock consumes an offering (Judges 6:21), as fire from heaven will here (21:26). Ornan's four sons hide at the sight of the angel, as people in the Bible usually fear a heavenly visitor (Judges 6:22–23; 13:22). The threshing season places the story in late spring or early summer. 4QSam-a is reported to share the detail about threshing wheat (see the variant on 2 Samuel 24:20).

a: for its full price in silver
p: David uses the exact phrase Abraham used when he bought the cave of Machpelah.
b: The Hebrew bekhesef male, "for full silver," appears only here, in 21:24 and in Genesis 23:9, where Abraham asks to buy the cave "at its full price in silver." Samuel does not have the phrase. By using it, the Chronicler sets the temple site beside the patriarchs' grave: both were bought openly at full price, so that no one could later claim them. See the note on 2 Samuel 24:24. Kesef means both "silver" and "money," so the phrase need not clash with 21:25, where David pays in gold.

a: and the wheat for the grain offering
p: Chronicles adds the wheat. Ornan offers the place, the animals, the fuel and the grain.
b: In Samuel, Araunah offers oxen and wood (2 Samuel 24:22). Chronicles adds the wheat he was threshing, "for the grain offering" that went with burnt offerings (Numbers 15:1–10). His offer covers everything an altar service needed. David still refuses a gift for God that would cost him nothing.

a: David gave Ornan gold for the place
p: Samuel says fifty shekels of silver. Chronicles says six hundred of gold, 'for the place'.
b: Six hundred gold shekels weighed about 15 pounds (7 kg), many times the fifty silver shekels of 2 Samuel 24:24. Explanations: (1) Samuel's price was for the floor and the oxen, Chronicles' for the whole site ("the place"), the later temple mount; (2) the Chronicler raised the price to honor the temple, as he enlarges other numbers; (3) six hundred is twelve times fifty, perhaps a price for all twelve tribes. Chronicles' word maqom, "place," is also the word Deuteronomy uses for "the place the LORD your God will choose" (Deuteronomy 12:5).

a: fire came from heaven onto the altar of burnt offering
p: God's fire shows that he accepts a new altar, as at the tabernacle, on Carmel and at Solomon's temple.
b: Samuel ends with God accepting the prayers for the land (2 Samuel 24:25). Chronicles adds fire from heaven, the sign God gave when worship began at the tabernacle ("Fire came out from before the LORD and ate up the burnt offering," Leviticus 9:24), for Gideon (Judges 6:21), for Elijah (1 Kings 18:38) and again at the temple's dedication (2 Chronicles 7:1). The fire marks David's altar as the true successor of Moses' altar, though it stands far from the tabernacle (21:29).

a: he returned his sword to its sheath
p: The image closes the story and is echoed in Jeremiah and by Jesus.
b: Only now does the threat of 21:16 end. Jeremiah's lament asks the LORD's sword how long before it goes back to its sheath (Jeremiah 47:6), and Ezekiel's sword song pictures the reverse (Ezekiel 21:3–5). Jesus tells Peter to put his sword back in its sheath (John 18:11). In Chronicles the sheathed sword marks the change from judgment to mercy at the place where the temple will stand.

a: stood at the high place in Gibeon
p: The official altar was at Gibeon. Chronicles explains why David sacrificed somewhere else.
b: Chronicles alone says that Moses' tabernacle and bronze altar stood at Gibeon, served by Zadok (16:39–40), and that Solomon went there to worship (2 Chronicles 1:3–6). The Law insisted on one altar (Leviticus 17:8–9; Deuteronomy 12:13–14). So the writer explains how a second altar could be legitimate: God commanded it through his angel and prophet, answered it with fire, and David was too afraid of the angel's sword to go to Gibeon. The explanation prepares for the single temple altar that will replace both.

a: The sword of the LORD's angel had filled him with terror
p: The verb ba'at means sudden terror, the kind Saul felt from the evil spirit.
b: Niv'at is the word for panic. An evil spirit terrified Saul (1 Samuel 16:14), Haman was terrified before the king and queen (Esther 7:6), and Daniel was terrified when Gabriel came near (Daniel 8:17). The angel's sword still stands between David and the old sanctuary. Many readers think this verse and 22:1 belong together: unable to go to Gibeon, David names the threshing floor as God's house.

a: This is the house of the LORD God
p: David names the place as Jacob named Bethel: 'This is nothing but the house of God'.
b: Jacob woke from his dream and said, "This is nothing but the house of God, and this is heaven's gate" (Genesis 28:17). David's words have the same shape: "This is the house of the LORD God, and this is the altar." A place where God has met someone in fear becomes a place of worship. Samuel never says that Araunah's floor became the temple's site; Chronicles does here and in 2 Chronicles 3:1, where it is called Mount Moriah, the name of the land where Abraham was told to offer Isaac (Genesis 22:2).

a: the foreigners living in the land of Israel
p: The gerim, the resident foreigners, are drafted as stonecutters, as in Solomon's labor gangs.
b: Gerim are foreigners who live in Israel without land of their own; the Law protects them (Exodus 22:21; Leviticus 19:33–34). Here David enrolls them as labor. 2 Chronicles 2:17–18 says Solomon counted 153,600 of them for the same work, and Kings says Solomon drafted the surviving Canaanite peoples (1 Kings 9:20–22). Many scholars see Chronicles sparing Israelites from the forced labor that 1 Kings 5:13–14 says Solomon imposed on all Israel.

a: iron in plenty
p: Iron was coming into common use in the 1000s and 900s BC.
b: The Philistines had kept Israel from working iron (1 Samuel 13:19–22). By the 900s BC iron tools and weapons were common across the region, and iron nails and fittings are known from excavations. The great stores of bronze recall the plunder David took from Hadadezer's towns (18:8), which Chronicles says Solomon used for the bronze sea and pillars.

a: the people of Sidon and Tyre had brought David great loads of cedar
p: Phoenician cedar went into the first temple and the second.
b: The cedars of Lebanon were the finest building timber of the ancient Near East, sought by Egyptian and Mesopotamian kings. Hiram of Tyre had already sent David cedar for his palace (14:1), and 1 Kings 5 tells how Solomon traded grain and oil for it. When the exiles rebuilt the temple, they too paid "the people of Sidon and Tyre" to bring cedar by sea to Joppa (Ezra 3:7), so the Chronicler's readers knew the arrangement well.

a: young and tender
p: The Bible never gives Solomon's age at accession. Josephus implies fourteen.
b: Na'ar varakh, "young and tender," is said of Solomon again in 29:1, and of Rehoboam (2 Chronicles 13:7). At Gibeon Solomon says, "I am only a youngster" (1 Kings 3:7), a common way of showing humility. Josephus gives him an eighty-year reign and ninety-four years of life, which would make him fourteen at his accession (Antiquities 8.211), but this is a late estimate. Since Rehoboam was forty-one at Solomon's death after a forty-year reign (1 Kings 14:21; 11:42), Solomon was probably at least in his late teens or older.

a: David got a great deal ready before he died
p: Kings gives the temple to Solomon alone. Chronicles makes David its true founder.
b: In 1 Kings, Solomon gathers the materials, organizes the work and plans the building (1 Kings 5–7). Chronicles gives chapters 22–29 to David's preparations: materials, workers, the Levites' duties and the written pattern (28:11–19). Solomon builds what David prepared, as Joshua finished what Moses began. Traditional readers take both accounts as true, Kings telling the building and Chronicles the planning. Critical scholars see the Chronicler giving the temple and its worship the authority of David, the founder of the dynasty, for readers rebuilding temple life after the exile.

a: You have shed blood in plenty
p: Each book gives a different reason why David did not build the temple. Chronicles names the blood he shed.
b: In 2 Samuel 7:5–7 God says he has never asked for a house of cedar. In 1 Kings 5:3 Solomon says David "could not build a house... because of the war that closed in around him." Chronicles has God say that David has shed much blood (also 28:3). Readers take this in several ways: (1) moral: even just wars stain the one who fights them; (2) ritual: shed blood makes a person unfit to found a holy place, as Numbers 35:33–34 says blood defiles the land; (3) typological: the temple belongs to an age of peace, so a man of rest must build it (22:9). Some compare the rule that no iron tool may touch the altar's stones (Exodus 20:25; Deuteronomy 27:5), which the Mishnah explains: iron was made to shorten life, and the altar to lengthen it (Mishnah Middot 3:4).

a: He will be a man of rest
p: Menuchah, 'rest', is a key word: the temple is built when God gives the land rest.
b: Deuteronomy promised that when God gave Israel "rest from all your enemies around you" (Deuteronomy 12:10), he would choose a place for his name. Chronicles sees that rest arriving with Solomon. David is a man of wars (28:3); Solomon is a man of rest (menuchah), and the temple itself is "a resting house" for the ark (28:2). Hebrews 4 later reads "rest" as something still to come for God's people.
orig: אִישׁ מְנוּחָה (ish menuchah), 'a man of rest'

a: Solomon will be his name
p: Shelomoh, Solomon, sounds like shalom, 'peace'.
b: God plays on the name: Shelomoh will be his name, and shalom, "peace," God will give. Nathan also gave him the name Jedidiah, "loved by the LORD" (2 Samuel 12:25). Jerusalem's name was heard as "city of peace" in later tradition (compare Psalm 122:6–7; Hebrews 7:2 on Salem). Christians have seen Solomon as a picture of the "Prince of Peace" (Isaiah 9:6).

a: He will be a son to me, and I will be a father to him
p: David quotes the promise of 17:13, and 2 Samuel 7:14, to Solomon.
b: David passes on Nathan's oracle (17:11–14), but now names Solomon as the son. Samuel's form, "I will be a father to him, and he will be a son to me" (2 Samuel 7:14), goes on to speak of punishing the son if he does wrong; Chronicles never repeats that warning. The New Testament applies the words to Jesus (Hebrews 1:5), and Paul extends them to all believers (2 Corinthians 6:18). See the topic on God's covenant with David.

a: good sense and understanding
t: The gift Solomon would ask for
p: David prays for the kind of gift Solomon later asks for at Gibeon.
b: David's prayer for sekhel uvinah, "good sense and understanding," anticipates the wisdom Solomon will ask for at Gibeon (2 Chronicles 1:10; 1 Kings 3:9), and God's answer, "a heart that is wise and understanding" (1 Kings 3:12). Kings ties Solomon's wisdom to judging the people; Chronicles, characteristically, ties it to keeping "the law of the LORD."

a: Be strong and bold
p: David's words to Solomon follow the pattern of Moses' charge to Joshua.
b: Moses told Joshua, "Be strong and bold. Do not be afraid ... and do not be shaken" (Deuteronomy 31:6–8), and God repeated it (Joshua 1:6–9). The same formula returns in 28:10 and 28:20. Dennis McCarthy called this an "installation" form: encouragement, a task, and a promise of God's presence. H. G. M. Williamson showed that Chronicles shapes the handover from David to Solomon on the handover from Moses to Joshua: the leader who could not finish the work names a successor who will.

a: in my hard times
t: In poverty, trouble or great effort?
p: Be'onyi can mean 'in my affliction', 'in my poverty' or 'with great pains'.
b: The word 'oni usually means affliction or misery (Genesis 41:52; Psalm 25:18). Older English Bibles have "in my trouble" (KJV), linking it to David's hard life of war. Others take it as "in my poverty," a humble way of speaking about an enormous gift, or "with great effort." Others connect it with Psalm 132:1–5, where David's "hardship" (from the same root) is his vow not to rest until he found a place for the LORD.

a: a hundred thousand talents of gold and a million talents of silver
p: About 3,400 tons of gold and 34,000 tons of silver. Readers explain the figures in three ways.
b: A talent weighed about 75 pounds (34 kg). These figures are far beyond anything known from the ancient world: Solomon's whole yearly income was 666 talents of gold (1 Kings 10:14), and the Assyrian king Sennacherib took thirty talents of gold from Hezekiah (2 Kings 18:14). (1) Literal: some traditional readers take them as given and point to the wealth David plundered (18:7–11). (2) Hyperbole: many readers, conservative and critical, see a deliberate way of saying "more than anyone could count," like 22:4 and 22:16. (3) Copying: some think numbers grew in transmission. Most commentators prefer the second. Compare the gifts in 29:4–7.

a: Hasn't he given you rest on all sides?
p: The words echo Joshua: the land 'has been brought under' the LORD and his people.
b: "The land has been brought under" (nikhbeshah) repeats the language of the conquest: at Shiloh, "The land had been brought under their control" (Joshua 18:1); compare Numbers 32:22, 32:29. In the Chronicler's eyes David finishes what Joshua began, so the time for the permanent sanctuary has come. The same leaders who fought with David are now told to build.

a: to seek the LORD your God
p: Darash, 'seek', is the Chronicler's favorite word for true religion.
b: To "seek" God (darash) in Chronicles means to turn to him in worship, prayer and obedience. Saul died because he did not seek the LORD (10:13–14); good kings seek him (2 Chronicles 14:4; 15:12; 17:4); God lets himself be found by those who seek (28:9; 2 Chronicles 15:2). Here seeking God and building his house go together. The word appears dozens of times in Chronicles.

a: He put his son Solomon on Israel's throne as king
p: One line stands in for the palace drama of 1 Kings 1, where Adonijah nearly takes the throne.
b: 1 Kings 1 tells how the old, bedridden David was moved by Nathan and Bathsheba to name Solomon while Adonijah held a feast to make himself king. Chronicles says nothing of the struggle. This verse works as a heading for chapters 23–29, which end with Solomon made king "a second time" (29:22). Traditional readers see the Chronicler choosing to tell the orderly side of a real transfer. Critical scholars see a deliberate picture of a smooth, united succession, in which "all King David's sons" pledge loyalty (29:24).

a: from thirty years old and up
p: The Levites' starting age is thirty here, as in Numbers 4. Later in the chapter it is twenty.
b: Numbers 4:3 counts Levites from thirty to fifty for carrying the tabernacle; Numbers 8:24 sets the age at twenty-five; this chapter starts at thirty (23:3) but then says that by David's last words the count began at twenty (23:24, 23:27), the age used after the exile (Ezra 3:8; 2 Chronicles 31:17). Explanations: (1) David lowered the age when the Levites no longer carried heavy loads (23:26) and more workers were needed; (2) the chapter combines an older list with a later revision; (3) the ages applied to different tasks. The Talmud harmonizes Numbers by saying the five years from twenty-five to thirty were training (Bavli Hullin 24a).

a: thirty-eight thousand
p: 38,000 Levites is far more than any other list. Numbers counted 8,580 men of working age.
b: Numbers 4:48 counts 8,580 Levites aged thirty to fifty. After the exile only 341 Levites, singers and gatekeepers returned with Zerubbabel, not counting priests (Ezra 2:40–42), and Ezra had trouble finding any (Ezra 8:15). Some read the figure as "thirty-eight units" ('elef, see the census topic); others as an idealized number for a fully staffed temple. Its divisions in 23:4–5 (24,000, 6,000, 4,000, 4,000) are all round.

a: David said
p: The Hebrew has no verb of speaking here. The Plain English supplies 'David said'.
b: Verse 3 reports the count of the Levites, and verse 4 begins a list of duties with no speaker named. The next verse, though, speaks of "the instruments I have made" (23:5), so the words are David's. The KJV and others leave the speech unmarked until 23:5; the Plain English marks it here so that the reader is not surprised by the "I." The same is done at 28:19.

a: officials and judges
p: Chronicles gives Levites roles in the government and the courts, not only in worship.
b: Deuteronomy told Israel to appoint "judges and officials" (shoftim veshoterim) in every town (Deuteronomy 16:18) and gave Levites a part in hard cases (Deuteronomy 17:8–9). Chronicles assigns six thousand Levites to these jobs and names them in 26:29–32. Jehoshaphat's reform appoints Levites as judges in Jerusalem and as officials (2 Chronicles 19:8–11). Some scholars see the Chronicler's own day, when the temple staff ran much of Judah's local life.

a: the instruments I have made for praising him
p: Chronicles calls the temple instruments 'David's instruments'. Amos and a Psalm from Qumran remember him as their maker.
b: Chronicles speaks of "the instruments of David" (2 Chronicles 29:26–27; Nehemiah 12:36). Amos mocks those who "invent instruments of music like David" (Amos 6:5). A poem attributed to David in the Greek Psalter, Psalm 151, and in its Hebrew form in the Psalms Scroll from Qumran (11QPs-a), has David say that his hands made a harp. Cymbals, lyres and harps are named in 25:1, 25:6. Trumpets were played by priests (15:24; 16:6).

a: Gershon, Kohath and Merari
p: Numbers gave each clan part of the tabernacle to carry. Now they get duties in a house that stays put.
b: In Numbers the Kohathites carried the holy objects, the Gershonites the curtains and coverings, and the Merarites the frames and posts (Numbers 3:21–37; 4:1–33). With the ark at rest in Jerusalem, Chronicles keeps the three clans as the frame for a new organization: lists of family heads (23:7–23), the priestly line from Kohath through Aaron (23:13), and duties around the temple (23:28–32).

a: The sons of Shimei: Shelomoth, Haziel and Haran
p: Shimei's sons appear here and again in 23:10. The first 'Shimei' was probably once another name.
b: Verse 9 gives sons of Shimei and then calls them "heads of the families of Ladan"; verse 10 lists the sons of Shimei a second time. Many scholars think that in verse 9 the original read "the sons of Jehiel" or "of Ladan," and an early copyist repeated Shimei by mistake. The name of the first son is written Shelomoth and read Shelomith (see the variant). Genealogies like these were working records for temple duty, so such slips were natural.

a: Aaron was set apart to treat the most holy things as holy
t: Most holy things, or a most holy man?
p: The Hebrew can mean Aaron was set apart 'to consecrate the most holy things' or 'to be consecrated as most holy'.
b: Lehaqdisho qodesh qodashim is literally "to make it (or him) holy, holy of holies." Most translations (KJV, BSB) take it as Aaron's duty toward the most holy things: the offerings and objects only priests could touch (Numbers 18:9–10). Others, including several modern commentators, read it of Aaron himself: he was set apart "to be consecrated as most holy." Either way, the line draws the boundary that runs through these chapters: the Levites assist, but only Aaron's sons handle the most holy things (23:28, 23:32).

a: to bless in his name for all time
p: Blessing the people in the LORD's name was a priestly task from Numbers 6 onward.
b: God told Aaron's sons to bless Israel with the words "The LORD bless you and keep you" (Numbers 6:22–27). Deuteronomy gives the tribe of Levi the task of blessing in his name (Deuteronomy 10:8; 21:5). Two tiny silver scrolls from Ketef Hinnom in Jerusalem, from about 600 BC, carry a form of the blessing. In synagogues today, men descended from Aaron still pronounce it.

a: his sons were named with the tribe of Levi
p: Moses' descendants served as ordinary Levites. The priesthood went to his brother's line.
b: Moses' sons Gershom and Eliezer (Exodus 2:22; 18:3–4) were counted among the Levites, not the priests. One of Moses' grandsons, "Jonathan son of Gershom, son of Moses," became priest of the shrine at Dan (Judges 18:30), where a later scribe hung a small letter nun in the name to turn "Moses" into "Manasseh," sparing Moses the shame. In Chronicles a descendant of Gershom, Shebuel, is chief over the temple treasuries (26:24).

a: Kish's sons, their relatives, took them as wives
p: Eleazar's daughters married cousins, as Zelophehad's daughters did, to keep the family line.
b: When a man had only daughters, the Law let them inherit, but they were to marry within the clan so the land stayed in the tribe (Numbers 27:1–11; 36:1–12). Zelophehad's daughters "became the wives of their uncles' sons" (Numbers 36:11). Eleazar's daughters do the same here, so his family's place in the Levite roll passed through them to Kish's sons.

a: he lives in Jerusalem for all time
p: The verb shakan, 'dwell, settle', gave later Judaism its word for God's presence, Shekhinah.
b: With the ark in Jerusalem, David says, God "has settled" (vayyishkon) there for good, so the portable tabernacle (mishkan, from the same root) is no longer needed. Psalm 132:13–14 says the LORD chose Zion as his resting place forever. Solomon will ask whether God can truly make his home on earth (1 Kings 8:27). The rabbis' word for God's dwelling presence, Shekhinah, comes from this verb.

a: there is no more carrying of the tabernacle
t: A new job for the Levites
p: The Levites' old work, carrying the tabernacle, has ended. Chronicles gives them new work in the temple.
b: In Numbers, carrying the tabernacle and its furnishings through the wilderness was the Levites' main task (Numbers 4; 7:9). Once the ark had a fixed home, Chronicles says, David gave them a new role: guarding, cleaning, baking, singing and keeping records (23:28–32). Only the carrying of the ark itself stayed theirs (15:2). Many scholars see in this the Chronicler's argument for the Levites' place in the second temple, where their status was debated.

a: By David's last words
p: Chronicles attributes the lower age of twenty to David's 'last words'.
b: "David's last words" in 2 Samuel 23:1–7 are a poem about a righteous ruler. Here the phrase refers to David's last decrees, perhaps the speeches of chapters 28–29. The verse explains why Levites were counted from twenty (see the note on 23:3). Many scholars think it is a later addition that updates the older figure of thirty in 23:3.

a: the rows of bread
p: Twelve loaves were set out in two rows each Sabbath on a gold table in the holy place.
b: The "bread of the row" (lechem hamma'arekhet) is the bread of the presence, set out in two rows of six on the gold table each Sabbath and eaten by the priests (Leviticus 24:5–9; Exodus 25:30). Chronicles says Kohathite Levites prepared it (9:32). Jesus cited David eating it at Nob (1 Samuel 21:6; Mark 2:25–26). The Levites also measured the flour and baked the flat cakes for grain offerings (Leviticus 2:4–7).

a: Morning after morning they were to stand and give thanks and praise to the LORD
t: Praise at the hours of sacrifice
p: Songs of praise went with the morning and evening offerings. Jewish prayer times grew from this rhythm.
b: The daily burnt offering was made morning and evening (Exodus 29:38–42; Numbers 28:3–8). Chronicles adds Levites standing to sing at those hours (also 16:37–42; 2 Chronicles 29:25–30). After the temple was destroyed in AD 70, the morning and afternoon prayers of the synagogue took the place of these offerings (Bavli Berakhot 26b). Psalm 92, "A Song for the Sabbath Day," speaks of declaring God's love in the morning and his faithfulness at night.

a: the Sabbaths, the New Moons and the set feasts
p: The list follows Numbers 28–29, the calendar of public offerings.
b: Numbers 28–29 sets the burnt offerings for each day, Sabbath, first of the month and festival. Chronicles repeats the three-part list (also 2 Chronicles 2:4; 8:13; 31:3), and Paul names the same three, "a festival, a new moon or Sabbaths" (Colossians 2:16). The New Moon marked the start of each month in a calendar that followed the moon.

a: Nadab and Abihu died while their father was still living
p: Aaron's two eldest sons died offering 'strange fire'. The priesthood passed through his two younger sons.
b: Nadab and Abihu offered unauthorized fire and were consumed by fire from the LORD (Leviticus 10:1–2; Numbers 3:4). Numbers adds that they had no sons, so all later priests traced their line to Eleazar or Ithamar. The Hebrew lifne avihem can mean "before their father" in time or "in their father's presence" (Numbers 3:4 says Eleazar and Ithamar served "in the presence of Aaron their father").

a: Zadok from Eleazar's sons and Ahimelech from Ithamar's sons
p: Chronicles traces Zadok to Eleazar and Abiathar's family to Ithamar. Scholars debate Zadok's real origins.
b: Chronicles gives Zadok a line back to Eleazar (6:3–8, 6:50–53) and makes Ahimelech, of Eli's house, a descendant of Ithamar. Solomon later sent Abiathar away and made Zadok sole chief priest (1 Kings 2:26–27, 2:35), fulfilling the word against Eli's house (1 Samuel 2:30–35). Samuel never gives Zadok a family line, and some scholars think he came from Jerusalem's older priesthood, perhaps a Jebusite; others accept the genealogy. Ezekiel limits altar service to "the sons of Zadok" (Ezekiel 44:15).

a: The division was made by lot
p: Lots left the choice to God and kept the larger house from taking the best turns.
b: Drawing lots was believed to leave a decision to God: "People throw the lot into the lap, / but every verdict it gives comes from the LORD" (Proverbs 16:33). It divided the land under Joshua (Joshua 14:2), chose Saul (1 Samuel 10:20–21) and later Matthias (Acts 1:26). Here it mixes the sixteen houses of Eleazar with the eight of Ithamar so that neither family controls the calendar. Luke says Zechariah was chosen by lot to burn incense (Luke 1:9).

a: Ahimelech son of Abiathar
p: Elsewhere Abiathar is Ahimelech's son. Here and in 2 Samuel 8:17 the names are reversed.
b: Abiathar, son of Ahimelech of Nob, escaped Saul's massacre and joined David (1 Samuel 22:20). He served with Zadok through David's reign (2 Samuel 15:24–29; 1 Kings 1:7). Yet 2 Samuel 8:17 and 1 Chronicles 18:16 (where the Masoretic Text has Abimelech, and many Hebrew manuscripts and the versions read Ahimelech), and these verses (24:3, 24:6, 24:31), name "Ahimelech son of Abiathar" as priest. Either Abiathar named a son after his father, or an early copy of 2 Samuel 8:17 reversed the names and Chronicles followed it. Mark 2:26 speaks of the bread at Nob being eaten "when Abiathar was high priest," though 1 Samuel 21 names Ahimelech.

a: One family was taken for Eleazar, then another taken for Ithamar
p: The Hebrew says 'one taken for Eleazar, and taken, taken for Ithamar'. Its pattern is unclear.
b: The repeated 'achuz, "taken," may describe the drawing: one lot from Eleazar's urn, then one from Ithamar's, alternating. Since Eleazar had sixteen houses and Ithamar eight, some suggest two lots for Eleazar for each one for Ithamar. Others correct the text to "one for Eleazar and one for Ithamar." The list itself (24:7–18) does not say which house received which turn.

a: The first lot came out for Jehoiarib
p: The twenty-four courses served into the first century AD. The Maccabees came from the first.
b: Mattathias, father of Judas Maccabeus, was "a priest of the line of Joarib" (1 Maccabees 2:1), the first course. Josephus, himself a priest, says he belonged to the first of the twenty-four courses (Life 1–2) and that the system lasted to his day (Antiquities 7.365–366). Calendar texts from Qumran (4Q320–330) schedule the courses week by week. An inscription from a synagogue in Caesarea, about AD 300, lists the courses with the towns in Galilee where their families settled after AD 70.

a: the eighth for Abijah
p: John the Baptist's father served in this course when the angel appeared to him.
b: "There was a priest named Zechariah, of the division of Abijah" (Luke 1:5). Luke says he was serving "in the order of his division" when the lot fell to him to burn incense (Luke 1:8–9). Some Christian scholars have tried to fix the date of Jesus' birth from the timing of Abijah's turn, but the starting point of the cycle is unknown, and the results disagree.

a: This was the order in which they served
p: Each course served a week at a time, about twice a year, and all served at the great feasts.
b: Later sources describe a weekly rotation, changing on the Sabbath (2 Chronicles 23:8; 2 Kings 11:5–9), so each course served about two weeks a year plus the pilgrim festivals. The Mishnah adds that each priestly course was matched by a group of ordinary Israelites, the ma'amad, who stood in the temple or prayed in their towns during its week (Mishnah Taanit 4:2). Many scholars date the full twenty-four-course system after the exile, since Nehemiah's lists have about twenty-two names, some matching these (Nehemiah 12:1–21).

a: As for the rest of Levi's descendants
p: This list repeats 23:12–23 and adds one more generation, matching the priests' order.
b: The names follow the Kohathite and Merarite families of 23:12–23 but go one step further (Shubael's son Jehdeiah, Shelomoth's son Jahath and so on). Gershonites are missing. Verse 31 says these Levite families also cast lots like the priests, which suggests an attempt to give the Levites a parallel set of courses. Many scholars see this as a later addition by the temple's own scribes.

a: Beno
p: Beno, here and in 24:27, may not be a name at all. In Hebrew it means 'his son'.
b: Beno is written exactly like the common word "his son." Most translations treat it as a name, but an alternative reading recorded for the Leningrad Codex, and many commentators, read "Jaaziah his son," making Jaaziah a third son of Merari besides Mahli and Mushi. Verse 27 would then read "of Jaaziah his son: Shoham, Zaccur and Ibri." Jaaziah appears nowhere else.

a: The head family was treated the same as the family of its youngest brother
p: Seniority gave no advantage. The lot treated senior and junior families alike.
b: The same rule returns for the singers, "the small the same as the great" (25:8), and the gatekeepers (26:13). In a world where firstborn rights mattered a great deal (Deuteronomy 21:17), the Chronicler stresses that in God's service no family outranked another in the order of duty.

a: who prophesied with lyres, harps and cymbals
p: Chronicles calls the temple music 'prophesying'. Readers differ on what that meant.
b: The Levite singers "prophesied" with instruments (25:1–3), and Heman is "the king's visionary" (25:5). Bands of prophets played music in Samuel's day (1 Samuel 10:5), and Elisha called for a musician before speaking (2 Kings 3:15). (1) Some see inspired song: the singers composed and sang psalms under God's Spirit, and 2 Chronicles 20:14 has a Levite of Asaph's line prophesy in the assembly. (2) Others see the word stretched to mean praise led by trained musicians. (3) Many critical scholars think the Chronicler's temple singers claimed the prophets' authority for their work and their psalms. Christians and Jews alike have treasured the psalms of Asaph, Heman and the sons of Korah as inspired Scripture.

a: the commanders of the army
t: Army commanders, or leaders of the service?
p: Sare hatstsava usually means army commanders, but tsava can also mean the Levites' service.
b: It is odd for army officers to organize temple music. But tsava, usually "army," is also the word for Levite "service" in Numbers 4:3, 4:23 and 8:24–25. So some translate "the chiefs of the service" (so ESV). Others keep "commanders of the army" (KJV "captains of the host," NIV, BSB), since David's officers appear in 28:1 too.

a: Asaph
t: Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun in the Psalms
p: Twelve psalms carry Asaph's name. Heman and Jeduthun also appear in psalm titles.
b: Psalms 50 and 73–83 are "of Asaph." Psalm 88 is "of Heman the Ezrahite," and Psalms 39, 62 and 77 mention Jeduthun. The "sons of Korah" of Psalms 42, 44–49, 84–85 and 87–88 are the Korahite Levites of 6:33–38 and 9:19. Asaph's descendants were among the singers who came back from exile (Ezra 2:41). Whether the titles name authors, collections or performers is discussed on the psalm-titles topic.

a: Hananiah, Hanani, Eliathah, Giddalti, Romamti-ezer, Joshbekashah, Mallothi, Hothir and Mahazioth
p: Heman's last nine sons' names, read in a row, sound like lines of a psalm.
b: Scholars have long noticed that the names, with slight changes, read: "Be gracious to me, LORD, be gracious to me; you are my God; I have made great and lifted high help; sitting in hardship, I have uttered; he gave plenty of visions" (roughly channeni yah channeni eli attah giddalti veromamti 'ezer yoshev beqashah malloti hotir machazi'ot). Some think the names were taken from the opening words of a psalm or a list of tunes; others that a singer family gave its sons names from its songs. The idea is old and widely accepted, but the details of the reconstruction are uncertain.

a: the king's visionary
p: Heman is called the king's chozeh, as Gad was David's visionary (21:9).
b: 2 Chronicles 35:15 calls Heman, Asaph and Jeduthun "the king's visionary." A Heman "the Ezrahite" is named as a famous wise man in 1 Kings 4:31 and in the title of Psalm 88; whether he is this Levite singer is debated, since Chronicles traces this Heman to Kohath (6:33). Fourteen sons and three daughters (compare Job's seven sons and three daughters, Job 42:13) show God's blessing.

a: to lift up his horn
p: An idiom for giving someone strength and honor, like a bull raising its horns.
b: Hannah sang, "my horn is raised high by the LORD" (1 Samuel 2:1), and that God would "raise high his anointed one's horn" (1 Samuel 2:10); compare Psalm 89:17, 89:24 and 92:10. Here the many sons are God's way of honoring Heman. A few scholars take qeren literally, "to blow the horn," a musical duty, but the honor reading fits the next clause.

a: two hundred and eighty-eight
p: Twenty-four groups of twelve singers each, matching the twenty-four priestly courses.
b: The total equals the twenty-four lots of 25:9–31, each with twelve men. The singers' system mirrors the priests' twenty-four courses (24:7–18) and the twelve monthly army divisions (27:1–15). The pattern of twelves and twenty-fours shows an ordered world around the temple. Revelation's twenty-four elders, holding harps and bowls of incense (Revelation 5:8), have often been read against this background.

a: the master the same as the pupil
p: The temple singers trained apprentices. The lot made no difference between them.
b: The word mevin, "one who understands," is the trained master (also 15:22; 25:7), and talmid, "learner," is used only here in the Hebrew Bible; it later became the rabbinic word for a student, and its Greek equivalent, mathetes, is the New Testament "disciple." Music was learned in families and guilds, from master to pupil.

a: for Joseph
p: The Hebrew gives no count for Joseph, the first lot. The Greek supplies 'his sons and brothers, twelve'.
b: Every other lot (25:9–31) ends with "twelve," and the total of 288 (25:7) needs twelve for Joseph too. The Masoretic Text lacks the phrase for Joseph; the Greek has it, and many translations add it. A scribe probably skipped from "Joseph" to the next entry. See the variant.

a: From the Korahites came Meshelemiah son of Kore
p: The Korahites, sons of the rebel Korah, became gatekeepers and singers.
b: Korah led a revolt against Moses and Aaron and died in it (Numbers 16), but "the sons of Korah did not die" (Numbers 26:11). Their descendants guarded the tabernacle's entrance (9:19) and sang in the temple. A psalm of the sons of Korah says, "I choose to stand at the threshold of my God's house rather than to live in the tents of the wicked" (Psalm 84:10). Meshelemiah is probably the Shelemiah of 26:14 and the Shallum of 9:17–19, and "Asaph" here is likely Ebiasaph (9:19).

a: Obed-edom
p: Samuel calls him 'Obed-edom the Gittite', a man from Gath. Chronicles counts his family among the Levites.
b: The ark stayed three months in Obed-edom's house, and the LORD blessed him (2 Samuel 6:10–12; 1 Chronicles 13:13–14). "Gittite" usually means from Gath, the Philistine city. Chronicles places Obed-edom among the Levite gatekeepers and singers (15:18, 15:24; 16:38) and gives him a large family. Some explain "Gittite" by Gath-rimmon, a Levite town (Joshua 21:24–25); others think there were two men of the name, or that the Chronicler took the ark's host into the Levites because only Levites could keep the ark. The verse's last words, "God had blessed him," point back to 13:14.

a: they cast lots for each gate
p: Gatekeepers controlled who came into the temple and guarded its stores.
b: Gatekeepers were the temple's guards. They kept the unclean out (2 Chronicles 23:19), opened the doors each morning (9:27), and watched the storehouses where offerings and treasure were kept (9:26; 26:15). In the second temple they were a distinct Levite group (Ezra 2:42; Nehemiah 11:19). The four directions of 26:14–18 add up to twenty-four posts (26:17–18).

a: a counselor with insight
p: Zechariah, guard of the north gate, was known as a counselor.
b: Zechariah son of Meshelemiah already kept the entrance of the tent of meeting (9:21). Calling him yo'ets besekhel, "a counselor with insight," suggests the gatekeepers also gave advice or settled disputes at the gate, where judging was done in Israel (Deuteronomy 21:19; Ruth 4:1).

a: Shuppim
p: The name may be an accidental repeat of the last word of verse 15, asuppim, 'storehouse'.
b: Verse 15 ends with ha'asuppim, "the storehouse"; verse 16 begins leshuppim, "for Shuppim." The words look much alike, and no Shuppim appears among the gatekeepers in 26:1–11. Many scholars think a copyist wrote the word twice and then read it as a name. The Greek supports them: it has Hosah alone, with no Shuppim (see the variant on this verse). The Plain English keeps the name, as most translations do.

a: the Shallecheth Gate on the road that goes up
p: The Shallecheth Gate is named only here. Its name may mean 'throwing out'.
b: Shallekhet comes from a verb meaning "to throw," so some think of a gate through which refuse was thrown out, or of a felled tree (Isaiah 6:13 uses the word). "The road that goes up" was probably a raised way or stairway from the city to the temple's west side, perhaps the "ascent" by which Solomon went up to the LORD's house (2 Chronicles 9:4).

a: the Parbar
p: A rare word, perhaps Persian, for a colonnade or courtyard on the temple's west side.
b: Parbar occurs only here, and in the plural parvarim in 2 Kings 23:11, where Josiah removed horses dedicated to the sun that stood "out in the Parbar" by the way into the LORD's house. Many scholars connect it with a Persian word for a porch or forecourt; others with an Aramaic word for "outer area." If it is Persian, it fits a text shaped in the Persian period, but the word may have entered Hebrew earlier.

a: Out of the wars and out of the plunder
p: War plunder was dedicated to God's house, as Moses' officers dedicated their gold after the war with Midian.
b: After the war with Midian the officers brought their gold: "So we bring the LORD a gift" (Numbers 31:50). David dedicated the silver and gold of the nations he defeated (18:10–11; 2 Samuel 8:11–12). The temple's treasuries thus held the record of Israel's victories, and later kings drew on them to buy off enemies (1 Kings 15:18; 2 Kings 18:15).

a: Samuel the seer, Saul son of Kish, Abner son of Ner and Joab son of Zeruiah
p: Chronicles usually passes over Saul in silence, but here names him with Samuel as a giver to the sanctuary.
b: Chronicles tells Saul's reign only through his death (chapter 10) and judges him harshly (10:13–14). Yet this list honors gifts from Samuel, Saul, Abner and Joab. It implies that a central treasury for the sanctuary existed before the temple, and it gives Samuel his title "the seer" (1 Samuel 9:9; 29:29). The list includes men who were bitter enemies (Abner and Joab, 2 Samuel 3:27), now joined as givers to one house.

a: the work outside, over Israel
p: Some Levite families served as officials and judges across the land.
b: Chenaniah's family worked "outside" the temple, as officials and judges (see the note on 23:4), and Hebronite Levites had charge of "every matter of God and every matter of the king" on both sides of the Jordan (26:30, 26:32). Jehoshaphat's courts use the same pair of terms (2 Chronicles 19:11). The Levites appear as the king's administrators as well as God's servants.

a: In the fortieth year of David's reign
p: The date sets chapters 23–27 in the last year of David's life.
b: David reigned forty years (29:27). Placing this search of the records in his fortieth year frames the whole organization of chapters 23–27 as David's final work, done after Solomon's appointment (23:1). Jazer in Gilead was a Levite town east of the Jordan (Joshua 21:39), so Levite families there were natural officials for the eastern tribes.

a: Each division had twenty-four thousand
p: Twelve divisions of 24,000 served a month each. The total, 288,000, is very large for David's kingdom.
b: The plan is a militia: each division served one month a year, so the whole force rotated through the year. (1) Traditional readers take the figures as given, a reserve army built on the tribes. (2) Some read 'elef here as a military unit rather than a thousand, giving twenty-four units per division (see the census topic). (3) Many critical scholars think the list is an idealized scheme built on the names of David's heroes (27:2–15) and the twelve months, with numbers meant to show order and strength, not a real roster. The 288,000 total has been compared with the 1,100,000 of 21:5.

a: Jashobeam son of Zabdiel
p: Nearly every commander here also appears in the list of David's mighty men (11:10–47; 2 Samuel 23:8–39).
b: Jashobeam (11:11), Dodai the Ahohite (father of Eleazar, 11:12), Benaiah (11:22–25), Asahel (11:26), Shamhuth (Shammoth, 11:27), Ira (11:28), Helez (11:27), Sibbecai (11:29), Abiezer (11:28), Maharai (11:30), Benaiah of Pirathon (11:31) and Heldai (Heled, 11:30) are all names from the heroes' list. Either the warriors went on to lead the militia, or a later writer used the famous names to fill out the scheme. Several spellings differ between Samuel and Chronicles (Heleb or Heled, Mebunnai or Sibbecai).

a: one of the descendants of Perez
p: Perez was Judah's son by Tamar, and David's own ancestor.
b: Perez was the son of Judah and Tamar (Genesis 38:29), the ancestor of Boaz and David (Ruth 4:18–22; 2:4–5). Jashobeam's descent makes the first commander, for the first month, a man of the king's own clan. In 11:11 and 12:6 a Jashobeam is called a Hachmonite and a Korahite, which may be different men of the same name.

a: Dodai the Ahohite, with his division, and Mikloth was the officer in charge
p: The verse reads awkwardly. In the heroes' list, Eleazar son of Dodo the Ahohite is the second hero.
b: "Eleazar son of Dodo the Ahohite" is second among David's three chief heroes (11:12; 2 Samuel 23:9). Many scholars think the words "Eleazar son of" dropped out here, so that the original read "Eleazar son of Dodai the Ahohite." The phrase "and his division, and Mikloth the officer in charge" may also be damaged; a Mikloth appears in Saul's family (8:32). The Plain English follows the Hebrew as it stands.

a: Benaiah son of Jehoiada the priest
p: The Hebrew can make Jehoiada 'the chief priest' or Benaiah 'chief' of the division.
b: The words hakkohen rosh may mean "Jehoiada the chief priest" or "Jehoiada the priest; (Benaiah was) chief." A Jehoiada led the house of Aaron when David became king at Hebron (12:27). Benaiah, a soldier from Kabzeel in Judah (11:22), commanded the king's bodyguard (18:17) and later executed Joab and became head of the army under Solomon (1 Kings 2:34–35).

a: Asahel the brother of Joab, with Zebadiah his son after him
t: A commander who was already dead
p: Asahel was killed by Abner before David ruled all Israel. The list adds his son after him.
b: Abner killed Asahel at Gibeon during the war between David and Saul's house (2 Samuel 2:18–23), years before David became king over all Israel. So either the division was named for him and led by his son, or the list goes back to David's early days in Hebron, or it is a later scheme built on famous names (see the note on 27:2). The phrase "and his son Zebadiah after him" seems meant to explain the problem.

a: In charge of Israel's tribes
p: The list names leaders for thirteen groups, including Aaron and both halves of Manasseh, but leaves out Gad and Asher.
b: The tribal list counts Levi and Aaron separately, and the two halves of Manasseh separately, but has no leader for Gad or Asher. Some think the writer wanted twelve names besides Aaron and dropped two to make room; others think two lines were lost in copying. Israel's tribal lists vary throughout the Bible (Genesis 49; Deuteronomy 33, which omits Simeon; Revelation 7:4–8, which omits Dan).

a: Elihu, one of David's brothers
p: No brother named Elihu appears elsewhere. The Greek reads Eliab, David's eldest brother.
b: David's brothers are listed in 2:13–15 and 1 Samuel 16:6–10, and none is called Elihu. The eldest was Eliab. The Greek of Chronicles reads "Eliab" here (see the variant), and many commentators accept it. Others note that 1 Samuel 16:10–11 counts eight sons of Jesse while 2:13–15 names seven, so there may have been a brother not listed. "Brother" can also mean a more distant relative.

a: as many as the stars in the sky
p: David did not count the young because God had promised descendants beyond counting.
b: God told Abraham, "Look toward the sky and number the stars, if you can number them" (Genesis 15:5), and promised offspring like the stars (Genesis 22:17; 26:4; Exodus 32:13). A full count would treat the promise as something to measure. Moses could already say, "Today you are like the stars of the sky in number" (Deuteronomy 1:10). The verse explains why the numbers in this chapter cover only men twenty and over, and it looks back to the census of chapter 21.
r: Genesis 15:5; Genesis 22:17; Genesis 26:4; Deuteronomy 1:10; Deuteronomy 10:22; Hebrews 11:12

a: Wrath fell on Israel over this
p: Chronicles links the army lists back to chapter 21: Joab never finished the count, and wrath came.
b: Joab's unfinished count matches 21:6, where he skipped Levi and Benjamin. The "wrath" is the plague of 21:14. The writer seems to want the reader to see that the military lists of this chapter do not come from the forbidden census.

a: the annals of King David
t: Divre hayyamim: the name of Chronicles
p: The Hebrew phrase is divre hayyamim, 'the words of the days', the Hebrew name of the book of Chronicles.
b: The Hebrew here is divre hayyamim, "the events of the days," which the Plain English renders "the annals." Kings repeatedly cites "the book of the events of the days of the kings" (sefer divre hayyamim, 1 Kings 14:19, 14:29). Royal courts kept such annals, as in Assyria and Babylon. In the Hebrew Bible, 1 and 2 Chronicles is called Divre Hayyamim, "the events of the days"; the English name comes from Jerome, who called it a "chronicle of the whole of sacred history." The Greek title is Paraleipomena, "things left out."

a: Azmaveth son of Adiel managed the king's treasuries
p: David's wealth came partly from royal farms, herds and storehouses run by stewards.
b: Ancient kings owned land, flocks and stores of grain, wine and oil, managed by officials. Kings mentions Solomon's district governors (1 Kings 4:7–19), and Samuel warned that a king would take fields and vineyards for himself (1 Samuel 8:14). Jar handles stamped "belonging to the king" (lmlk), from about 700 BC, show royal stores in Judah later. Each of the twelve stewards here oversees one kind of property.

a: the sycamore figs in the Shephelah
p: The sycamore fig, not the English sycamore, grew in the warm low hills west of Judah.
b: The Shephelah is the belt of low hills between the coastal plain and the hill country of Judah. Its sycamore fig (Ficus sycomorus) gave cheap fruit and light timber; Amos tended them (Amos 7:14), and Solomon made cedar as common as sycamores there (1 Kings 10:27). Olive trees produced the oil for food, lamps and anointing.

a: Obil the Ishmaelite oversaw the camels
p: An Ishmaelite in charge of camels and a Hagrite over flocks: desert peoples known for these animals.
b: The Ishmaelites were caravan traders with camels (Genesis 37:25), and the Hagrites were herders east of the Jordan whose flocks Israel had seized (5:10, 5:19–21). Putting them in charge of camels and flocks shows foreigners trusted in the king's service and fits their known skills. Obil's name may come from an Arabic word for camel herdsman.

a: David's uncle Jonathan
p: Dod usually means uncle. Some think this Jonathan is David's nephew, son of Shimea.
b: Dod means uncle (or more loosely, kinsman). A Jonathan son of Shimea, David's brother, killed a Philistine giant (20:7; 2 Samuel 21:21), and some identify him with this counselor. With Jehiel he looked after the king's sons, likely as tutor; "son of Hachmoni" may mean of the Hachmonite clan (11:11).

a: Ahithophel served as counselor to the king
p: The two men faced off during Absalom's revolt, which Chronicles never tells.
b: Ahithophel went over to Absalom; Hushai, "the king's friend," pretended to join Absalom and defeated Ahithophel's advice, and Ahithophel hanged himself (2 Samuel 15:12, 15:32–37; 17:1–23). Chronicles omits the revolt, but its list keeps both men. "The king's friend" was a court title, also held under Solomon (1 Kings 4:5), like "friend of the king" in Egypt.

a: Jehoiada son of Benaiah, and Abiathar
p: Ahithophel's place went to Jehoiada and Abiathar. The name may be Benaiah's father reversed.
b: Benaiah's father was Jehoiada (27:5), so many scholars think "Jehoiada son of Benaiah" is a slip for Benaiah son of Jehoiada, or a grandson named for his grandfather. Abiathar the priest also gave counsel. Joab, as always, commanded the army (11:6; 18:15).

a: David gathered to Jerusalem all of Israel's leaders
t: A strong David or a dying one?
p: In 1 Kings 1 David is old and bedridden. In Chronicles he stands before a great assembly.
b: 1 Kings 1 opens with David cold in bed and unable to keep warm, and he names Solomon from his bed. Here David summons all Israel's leaders and "stood up on his feet" (28:2) to speak. (1) Many traditional readers place these scenes at different times: the assembly came before David's last illness, or after Solomon's first anointing (29:22). (2) Many critical scholars see the Chronicler's ideal David: not a weak old man manipulated at court, but a founder handing over the kingdom and the temple plans in public.

a: for the footstool of our God's feet
p: God sits enthroned above the cherubim. The ark beneath is the footstool for his feet.
b: Psalm 99:5 and Psalm 132:7 call worshipers to bow at God's footstool, and Lamentations 2:1 mourns that God forgot "his footstool" when Jerusalem fell. Ancient thrones had footstools: one from Tutankhamun's tomb is decorated with his enemies, under the king's feet. Isaiah widens the picture: heaven is God's throne and the earth his footstool (Isaiah 66:1; Acts 7:49; Matthew 5:35). The ark is only the place where the invisible King rests his feet.
r: Psalm 99:5; Psalm 132:7; Lamentations 2:1; Isaiah 66:1; Acts 7:49; Matthew 5:35

a: a resting house for the ark
p: Psalm 132 sings of finding a resting place for the ark. Solomon's prayer quotes it.
b: Psalm 132 tells of David's vow not to rest until he found a dwelling for the LORD, and prays, "Up, LORD, to your place of rest, you and the ark of your strength!" (Psalm 132:8). Solomon ends his dedication prayer with those words in 2 Chronicles 6:41. The ark, which traveled through the wilderness looking for rest (Numbers 10:33), comes to rest at last.

a: He chose Judah to be ruler
p: God chose Judah, then Jesse's family, then David, then Solomon: a chain of choices.
b: Jacob's blessing promised that the scepter would not leave Judah (Genesis 49:10). Chronicles says Judah grew strongest among the tribes and "a ruler" came from him (5:2). Psalm 78:67–70 tells the same choice: God rejected Ephraim's tent and chose Judah, Mount Zion and David. Here David narrows it down step by step, and in 28:5 one step further, to Solomon. The word for ruler is nagid, the title God gave Saul and David (1 Samuel 9:16; 13:14).

a: the throne of the LORD's kingdom
p: In Chronicles the throne is not only David's but the LORD's. Israel's king sits on God's throne.
b: Chronicles changes Nathan's promise from "your kingdom" (2 Samuel 7:16) to "my kingdom" (17:14) and speaks of the throne as the LORD's (29:23; 2 Chronicles 9:8; 13:8). (1) Jewish readers see the king as God's steward, his rule valid only under God's law. (2) Christians hear the background of "the kingdom of God" in Jesus' preaching and of the Son of David on God's throne (Luke 1:32–33; Revelation 3:21). (3) Critical scholars note that when Chronicles was written there was no king in Judah at all; the idea kept hope for God's kingdom alive under Persian rule.

a: if he holds firm in doing my commands and my rulings
p: Here the kingdom depends on Solomon's obedience. Elsewhere the promise to David seems unconditional.
b: Nathan's oracle promised that God's loyal love would not leave David's son (2 Samuel 7:15; 17:13). Yet 28:7 and 28:9, like 1 Kings 2:4 and 9:4–7 and Psalm 132:12, attach a condition. Readers hold the two together in different ways: (1) the dynasty is secure, but each king can lose God's favor; (2) the promise is unconditional in the end and fulfilled in the Messiah; (3) critical scholars see two strands of thought, with the condition added after the exile had shown the dynasty could fall.

a: with all Israel watching, the LORD's assembly, and with our God listening
p: David speaks before two audiences, the assembly and God himself.
b: Calling God as listening witness is a feature of covenant speeches (Joshua 24:22, 24:27; Deuteronomy 30:19). The "assembly" (qahal) is a favorite word of Chronicles for all Israel gathered for worship; it gave the Greek ekklesia, the New Testament word for the church.

a: The LORD searches out every heart
p: The theme runs from Samuel to Revelation: God judges the inside, not the outside.
b: "A human sees what is before the eyes, but the LORD sees the heart" (1 Samuel 16:7). Jeremiah says God searches the heart and tests the inner being (Jeremiah 17:10). The New Testament repeats it: God "who searches the hearts" (Romans 8:27) and the risen Christ, who "searches minds and hearts" (Revelation 2:23). David will say the same in prayer (29:17).

a: every plan the thoughts form
p: Yetser, 'what is formed', is the word of Genesis 6:5. The rabbis built their idea of the 'evil inclination' on it.
b: Yetser machashavot, "the forming of thoughts," recalls Genesis 6:5, where every "inclination" of the human heart was evil, and Genesis 8:21. David uses the phrase again in prayer (29:18), and the Plain English renders it the same way there. Rabbinic teaching spoke of a good and an evil yetser, "inclination," in every person. The point here is that God sees not only deeds but the very forming of intentions.

a: Seek him, and he will let you find him
p: The promise returns throughout the Bible and becomes a theme of Chronicles' later kings.
b: Moses promised that Israel in exile would find God if they sought him with all their heart (Deuteronomy 4:29). The prophet Azariah tells Asa the same words (2 Chronicles 15:2), and Jeremiah writes to the exiles, "you will seek me and find me" (Jeremiah 29:13, in fresh wording). Jesus says, "seek, and you will find" (Matthew 7:7). In Chronicles the rest of the history tests this verse, king by king.

a: the pattern of the porch
p: Tabnit, 'pattern', is the word for the plan God showed Moses for the tabernacle.
b: God told Moses to make everything by "the pattern of the tabernacle and the pattern of all its furnishings" (Exodus 25:9) and "by their pattern, the one you are being shown on the mountain" (Exodus 25:40). David's tabnit makes the temple a second tabernacle, planned by God and not by human taste. Hebrews 8:5 reads the tabernacle pattern as a copy of a heavenly sanctuary.

a: the room for the atonement lid
t: The house of the atonement lid
p: Only here is the inner sanctuary called 'the house of the kapporet'.
b: The kapporet, "atonement lid," was the gold cover of the ark, where the high priest sprinkled blood on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:14–15). Naming the inner room after it makes atonement the center of the whole building. Kings and Chronicles elsewhere call it "the inner sanctuary" or "the most holy place" (1 Kings 6:16; 2 Chronicles 3:8).

a: everything he had in his spirit
t: In his mind, or by the Spirit?
p: Barruach immo, 'in the spirit with him', can mean David's own mind or God's Spirit.
b: Some translations read "all that he had in mind" (BSB, ESV); others "by the spirit" (KJV) or "that the Spirit had put in his mind" (NIV). The Hebrew ruach covers both. Read with 28:19, where David says the plan came "from the LORD's hand on me," many interpreters, Jewish and Christian, have taken it as revelation.

a: the gold lampstands
p: Solomon's temple had ten lampstands, not the single menorah of the tabernacle.
b: The tabernacle had one seven-branched lampstand (Exodus 25:31–40). Solomon made ten, five on each side (1 Kings 7:49; 2 Chronicles 4:7). Chronicles also mentions silver lampstands, not found in Kings. The second temple again had one menorah, carried off to Rome in AD 70 and carved on the Arch of Titus.

a: the pattern of the chariot
p: Only here are the ark's cherubim called a chariot. Ezekiel saw God's throne on living cherub-chariots.
b: The cherubim spread their wings over the ark (Exodus 25:20; 1 Kings 6:23–28), and God was "enthroned on the cherubim" (1 Samuel 4:4). Calling them a merkavah, "chariot," links the ark with the moving throne of Ezekiel 1 and 10 and with God riding on a cherub (Psalm 18:10). Ben Sira speaks of Ezekiel seeing "the chariot of the cherubim" (Sirach 49:8). Later Jewish mystics called their visions of God's throne "merkavah" teaching.
r: Exodus 25:18–22; 1 Samuel 4:4; Psalm 18:10; Ezekiel 1:4–28; Ezekiel 10:1–22; Sirach 49:8

a: All of it is in writing, from the LORD's hand on me
p: David claims a written plan from God: revelation, inspired design, or the writer's claim for his own temple?
b: The Hebrew has no verb of speaking here; the Plain English supplies "David said," since the words are his (compare "me" and 28:20). (1) Revelation as history: traditional Jewish and Christian readers take it at face value: as Moses received a pattern on the mountain (Exodus 25:9, 25:40), David received the temple's plan in writing. (2) Inspired planning: "the LORD's hand on me" is the prophets' phrase for being moved by God (Ezekiel 1:3; 2 Kings 3:15), so David drew it up under inspiration. (3) The writer's own time: many critical scholars think the Chronicler gave David the authority for the temple order of his own day, its Levites, singers and gatekeepers, so that it could not be questioned. The words "in writing" may also point to a written temple rule known to the Chronicler's readers.

a: He will not let you down, and he will not abandon you
p: David repeats Moses' promise to Joshua. Hebrews later applies it to every believer.
b: The words are exactly Moses' promise in Deuteronomy 31:6, 31:8 and God's in Joshua 1:5. Hebrews 13:5 quotes the promise to encourage Christians to be content with what they have. As Moses could not enter the land and handed the task to Joshua, David cannot build and hands the task to Solomon, with the same assurance that God will stay with him until the work is done. See the note on 22:13.

a: Every willing, skilled man
t: Willing workers, as for the tabernacle
p: Chronicles' David draws on the story of the tabernacle's free-hearted builders.
b: Moses called "every wise-hearted man" to make the tabernacle, and the people came willingly (Exodus 35:10, 35:21–29; 36:1–2). Chronicles uses nadiv, "willing," and the free-will giving of 29:5–9 for the same pattern. David and Solomon become a new Moses and Bezalel, and the temple a second tabernacle.

a: This citadel
p: Birah, 'citadel', is a word used mostly in books from the Persian period.
b: Birah appears in Nehemiah (1:1; 2:8; 7:2), Esther ("Susa the citadel," 1:2) and Daniel 8:2, and in Aramaic papyri from the Persian period. Here and in 29:19 it names the temple. Many scholars count it among the signs that Chronicles was written in the Persian age; Nehemiah 2:8 speaks of "the citadel of the temple," the fortress beside the second temple.

a: dark-set stones
p: Some of these stone names are uncertain. Avne fukh may be stones set in dark mortar or eye-paint.
b: Shoham is onyx or carnelian, set on the high priest's shoulder pieces (Exodus 28:9). Avne fukh, literally "stones of antimony" (the black eye-paint of 2 Kings 9:30), may be stones set in dark mortar, as in God's promise to rebuild Jerusalem with stones "in antimony" (Isaiah 54:11). Riqmah means varied colors, and shayish may be alabaster or white marble. Revelation's new Jerusalem is built of precious stones too (Revelation 21:18–21).

a: my own private treasure
p: Segullah is the word God used for Israel as his 'own private treasure'.
b: God called Israel "my own private treasure" (Exodus 19:5); Ecclesiastes 2:8 uses segullah for the private wealth of kings. David gives from his personal fortune, beyond what he had set aside from the kingdom (22:14), and so sets an example for the leaders (29:6–9).

a: gold of Ophir
p: Ophir was famous for fine gold. A Hebrew ostracon from Tell Qasile reads 'gold of Ophir'.
b: Solomon's ships brought gold from Ophir (1 Kings 9:28; 10:11), and "gold of Ophir" became a byword for the finest gold (Job 28:16; Psalm 45:9; Isaiah 13:12). A potsherd found at Tell Qasile, near Tel Aviv, from about the 700s BC, is inscribed "gold of Ophir for Beth-horon, thirty shekels." Ophir's location is unknown; suggestions include southern Arabia, the coast of East Africa and India.
r: 1 Kings 9:28; 1 Kings 10:11; Job 28:16; Psalm 45:9; Isaiah 13:12; Genesis 10:29

a: three thousand talents of gold
p: David's private gift alone is about 100 tons of gold. Readers take the numbers in different ways.
b: Three thousand talents of gold weigh about 100 metric tons; the leaders' gift of 29:7 adds about 170 tons more. As with 22:14, readers see literal figures, deliberate exaggeration of a lavish gift, or numbers enlarged in copying. For comparison, Solomon's yearly income in gold was 666 talents (1 Kings 10:14).

a: filling his hand with a gift for the LORD
p: The idiom 'fill the hand' usually means to ordain a priest. Here every giver is invited to consecrate himself.
b: To "fill the hand" of someone (mille' yad) is the Hebrew for ordaining a priest (Exodus 28:41; 29:9; Judges 17:5, 17:12; 1 Kings 13:33), perhaps from placing the first offering in his hands. David applies it to lay leaders: by giving, they too dedicate themselves to the LORD. In 2 Chronicles 29:31 Hezekiah uses it for the whole assembly.
orig: לְמַלֹּאות יָדוֹ (lemallo'ot yado), 'to fill his hand'

a: ten thousand darics
t: Darics: a sign of the Persian date?
p: The daric was a Persian gold coin, first struck under Darius I around 515 BC, five centuries after David.
b: The Hebrew adarkonim appears also in Ezra 8:27 (compare darkemonim in Ezra 2:69; Nehemiah 7:70–72). Coins did not exist in David's day; the first were struck in Lydia in the 600s BC. (1) Most scholars take the word as the Persian daric and see it as a sign that the Chronicler wrote after about 515 BC, translating the gift into money his readers knew. (2) Some think darkemon is the Greek drachma, which would point later still. (3) Traditional readers who hold an early date usually agree the term is the writer's own updating, like a modern historian giving ancient sums in dollars; it does not mean David used coins. Williamson and others use the word to place the book well into the Persian period.

a: they had given to the LORD of their own will, with a whole heart
p: Free, glad giving for God's house goes back to the tabernacle and forward to Paul.
b: At the tabernacle the people brought so much that Moses had to stop them: "The people are bringing too much, more than the service needs" (Exodus 36:5). The returned exiles also gave freely for the second temple (Ezra 2:68–69). Paul writes that "God loves a cheerful giver" (2 Corinthians 9:7, in fresh wording). The verb nadav, "give freely," appears seven times in 29:5–17.

a: Blessed are you, LORD
p: Jews recite 29:10–13 every morning, and 29:11 when the Torah scroll is carried out.
b: David's words open with barukh attah YHWH, "Blessed are you, LORD," the formula that begins every Jewish blessing (also Psalm 119:12). The section 29:10–13, called Vayevarekh David, "David blessed," is part of the daily morning service in the synagogue, and in many communities the congregation sings 29:11 as the Torah scroll is taken from the ark. Words from 29:14 are said in many churches when the offering is presented (see the note there).

a: Yours, LORD, is the kingdom
t: The source of the Lord's Prayer doxology
p: The ending many Christians add to the Lord's Prayer, 'for yours is the kingdom...', is modeled on this verse.
b: The oldest Greek manuscripts of Matthew end the Lord's Prayer with "deliver us from evil" (Matthew 6:13). Later manuscripts, and so the King James Version, add "For thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, for ever. Amen." A shorter form, "for yours is the power and the glory forever," already appears in the Didache, a Christian manual of about AD 100. Most scholars think the church added it for public worship, modeling it on David's prayer here, which names greatness, might, glory, kingdom and "over all." Defenders of the Byzantine text, such as Maurice Robinson, dissent and hold that the doxology belongs to Matthew's original. At Mass, Catholics say it as a separate line after the prayer; most Protestants say it as part of the prayer.
