a: the greatness and the might, the beauty, the victory and the majesty
p: The five Hebrew nouns, with 'everything' and 'the kingdom', later named seven of the Kabbalah's ten sefirot.
b: Gedullah (greatness), gevurah (might), tif'eret (beauty, glory), netsach (victory, or lastingness, splendor) and hod (majesty). Netsach is debated: it can mean lasting endurance (God is netsach yisrael, "Israel's Enduring One," 1 Samuel 15:29) or "victory" (so KJV). Medieval Jewish mystics took this verse as the source for the names of the seven lower sefirot of the ten, the powers through which God shows himself: the five nouns, "everything" (kol, read as Yesod, "foundation") and "the kingdom" (Malkhut).

a: Riches and glory have their source in you
p: God gave Solomon 'riches and glory' unasked. Moses warned Israel to remember who gives wealth.
b: "Riches and glory" (osher vekhavod) are what God promised Solomon though he did not ask for them (1 Kings 3:13), and David dies satisfied with them (29:28). Moses warned that when Israel grew rich, it must remember that the LORD gives the power to gain wealth (Deuteronomy 8:17–18). Hannah sang that the LORD makes poor and makes rich (1 Samuel 2:7).

a: What we have given you came out of your own hand
p: All giving is returning. The verse became a classic text on stewardship.
b: Jewish teaching quotes the idea: "Give him what is his, for you and what you have are his" (Mishnah Avot 3:7). Christian worship uses it too: many Anglican and Methodist services present the offering with words adapted from the KJV of this verse: "All things come of thee, O Lord, and of thine own have we given thee." The point is humility: God cannot be paid back, only thanked.

a: For we are foreigners before you, and lodgers
p: Even the king in his own land calls himself a resident foreigner before God.
b: Gerim vetoshavim is the pair God uses in Leviticus 25:23: "You are foreigners and lodgers living with me." Abraham said the same to the Hittites (Genesis 23:4), and a psalm prays, "I am a foreigner with you, a lodger, as all my fathers were" (Psalm 39:12). Hebrews says the patriarchs "admitted they were strangers and exiles on the earth" (Hebrews 11:13, in fresh wording), and 1 Peter 2:11 calls Christians foreigners and exiles. David's point: nothing we own is ours for good.

a: Like a shadow are our days on the earth, and there is no hope
t: No hope, or nothing that lasts?
p: Mikveh means hope or expectation. The KJV reads 'none abiding'. The sense is that life does not last.
b: Life as a passing shadow is a common image (Job 8:9; 14:2; Psalm 102:11; 144:4; Ecclesiastes 6:12). Mikveh usually means "hope" (Ezra 10:2; Jeremiah 14:8), so the line says there is no hope of staying on earth. The KJV has "there is none abiding," taking the word as "permanence." It is not a denial of hope in God, whom the prayer praises; it is a confession of human frailty.

a: you put the heart to the test
p: Jeremiah and the Psalms speak of God testing the heart and mind.
b: God "tests the heart" (bochen levav; Jeremiah 11:20; 17:10; 20:12; Psalm 7:9; Proverbs 17:3), and Paul writes that God tests our hearts (1 Thessalonians 2:4). David claims an honest heart in his giving and rejoices that the people gave the same way. Compare 28:9.

a: LORD, God of Abraham, Isaac and Israel, our fathers
p: Chronicles prefers 'Israel' to 'Jacob' for the third patriarch.
b: Chronicles almost always calls Jacob "Israel" (1:34; 2:1; 2 Chronicles 30:6), as Elijah does in his prayer on Carmel (1 Kings 18:36). The name stresses that the people are the sons of Israel, heirs of the promise. Jesus cites "the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob" as proof of resurrection (Matthew 22:32).

a: before the LORD and before the king
p: The same verb is used for worship and for honoring a king. It does not mean the king was worshiped.
b: Hishtachavah, "bow down, lie face down," was done before God and before human superiors: Abigail bowed to David (1 Samuel 25:23), and David's servants to him (1 Kings 1:47). Placing the LORD and the king together shows the Chronicler's picture of the king as God's representative on God's throne (29:23). Mordecai's refusal to bow to Haman (Esther 3:2) and the three young men's refusal to bow to the gold image (Daniel 3) show where later Jews drew the line.

a: a thousand young bulls, a thousand rams and a thousand lambs
p: Most of these were peace offerings, shared at a great meal 'before the LORD'.
b: The burnt offerings were burned whole, but the other "sacrifices" (zevachim) were peace offerings, eaten by the worshipers (Leviticus 7:11–15). So the next verse says they ate and drank. Solomon offered a thousand burnt offerings at Gibeon (1 Kings 3:4), and at the temple's dedication twenty-two thousand cattle and a hundred and twenty thousand sheep (1 Kings 8:63).

a: For a second time they made David's son Solomon king
p: The first time is 23:1 or the anointing at Gihon (1 Kings 1). Some Greek manuscripts lack the phrase.
b: Chronicles' own "first time" is 23:1. Many readers also connect the first time with the hurried anointing at Gihon during Adonijah's attempt (1 Kings 1:38–40), making this a public confirmation before the whole assembly. Some Greek manuscripts, and reportedly the Syriac, lack "a second time" (see the variant), and some scholars think a scribe added it to harmonize with 23:1 or with Kings.

a: and Zadok as priest
p: Chronicles alone says Zadok was anointed. Kings says Solomon put him in Abiathar's place.
b: "In Abiathar's place he put Zadok the priest" (1 Kings 2:35). Chronicles adds an anointing, so the high priest is installed together with the king, two anointed leaders side by side. Zechariah, after the exile, speaks of two "sons of oil," the governor Zerubbabel and the priest Joshua (Zechariah 4:14), and some scholars see that partnership mirrored here.

a: Solomon sat on the LORD's throne
t: On the throne of the LORD
p: Kings says Solomon sat on David's throne. Chronicles says the LORD's.
b: 1 Kings 2:12 reads, "Solomon sat on the throne of David his father." Chronicles keeps "David his father" but calls the throne the LORD's (see the note on 28:5). The Queen of Sheba says God placed Solomon "on his throne" (2 Chronicles 9:8), where 1 Kings 10:9 has "on Israel's throne."

a: and all King David's sons as well, gave their hand in pledge to King Solomon
p: Kings tells how Adonijah tried to take the throne. Chronicles says all David's sons pledged loyalty.
b: "Giving the hand under" someone is a gesture of submission or oath (compare 2 Chronicles 30:8; Ezra 10:19; Lamentations 5:6). In 1 Kings, Adonijah, David's eldest living son, made himself king, bowed to Solomon after failing, and was later executed (1 Kings 1:5–53; 2:13–25). Chronicles says nothing of this and pictures all the sons united. Traditional readers note that Adonijah did submit for a time (1 Kings 1:53); critical scholars see the Chronicler's idealized unity.

a: no king over Israel before him
p: Only Saul and David reigned before Solomon, so 'no king before him' is a modest claim, or a standard phrase.
b: The phrase echoes God's promise of unmatched riches and glory (1 Kings 3:12–13; 2 Chronicles 1:12). Since only two kings came before Solomon, some see it as a formula of praise rather than a comparison. 2 Chronicles 1:12 adds "nor after you."

a: forty years
p: Seven years in Hebron and thirty-three in Jerusalem. Samuel gives seven years and six months.
b: The figures repeat 1 Kings 2:11 almost word for word. 2 Samuel 5:5 gives seven years and six months in Hebron, so forty is rounded. Forty is also a round number for a generation in the Bible (Judges 3:11; 5:31), and Saul and Solomon are given forty years too (Acts 13:21; 1 Kings 11:42). Most historians date David's reign to about 1010–970 BC.

a: He died at a good old age, satisfied with days
p: David dies with the words used for Abraham and Isaac. Kings tells his death with no such praise.
b: Abraham "died at a good old age, old and satisfied" (Genesis 25:8), and Isaac was "old and satisfied with days" (Genesis 35:29); Job too dies "old and satisfied with days" (Job 42:17). 1 Kings 2:10 says only that David lay down with his ancestors. Chronicles gives David a patriarch's death, rich and honored, with his son already on the throne.

a: the accounts of Samuel the seer, the accounts of Nathan the prophet and the accounts of Gad the visionary
p: Chronicles cites three prophets as its sources for David. Most scholars think this means the books of Samuel.
b: The three titles are ro'eh (seer), navi (prophet) and chozeh (visionary), two of which 1 Samuel 9:9 explains. (1) The Talmud says Samuel wrote his book and Judges and Ruth, and Gad the visionary and Nathan the prophet finished it after his death (Bavli Bava Batra 14b–15a). (2) Many scholars think the Chronicler means our books of Samuel, in which these three prophets appear, and names them to stress that Israel's history was written by prophets. (3) Others think separate prophetic writings existed, now lost. Chronicles names similar prophetic sources for later kings (2 Chronicles 9:29; 12:15).

a: the times that swept over him
t: The times that passed over him
p: An idiom for the events and fortunes of a life.
b: Ha'ittim asher averu alav, "the times that passed over him," means all that happened to David, good and bad. The book closes his story by placing it among "all the kingdoms of the lands," since his fame had spread to every nation (14:17).
